title: ケニアの餓死カルト指導者に有罪判決

sources.headline: Kenya cult leader's children still being starved weeks before trial, son says
sources.text: Kenya cult leader's children still being starved weeks before trial, son saysImage source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Paul Mackenzie said education was forbidden and modern medicine was "evil"ByBasma El AttiReporting fromNairobiUpdated 14:23 BSTThe eldest son of Kenyan cult leader Paul Mackenzie, convicted of murdering 191 people, says his younger siblings were still being forced to fast as recently as two weeks ago.Dan Mackenzie, 27, said he reported the case to police, who rescued eight children, including his five younger siblings from their grandmother's house, and took them to a rescue centre."They were basically forcibly fasted because they were denying food to them for almost three days," he tells BBC's Newsday.His father was found guilty on Monday of murdering 190 children and one adult who starved to death in Shakahola forest, near the Kenyan coast.He had ordered members of his doomsday cult to starve themselves and their children to death so they could "meet Jesus".Twenty-eight other cult leaders were also convicted of murder. Dan Mackenzie, who had initially defended his father, said at first he had struggled to understand the allegations against the cult leader, but came to realise the scale of the tragedy during the court proceedings."When I was 12, I was forced to fast for almost a week," he says. He also remembers church members beating him for hours to make him attend a service as a child. Now, he says he felt he had to report family members who still believe in the teachings in order to free his siblings. "I had to report my grandmother."The cult leader's doctrine said that education was forbidden and modern medicine was "evil"."I left school when I was seven," says Dan.Now living in the coastal town of Malindi, Dan earns a living as a motorcycle taxi driver, supporting himself and his younger siblings.He said some people in the town had been angry with him because of his father's crimes, but others "had accepted him because he had distanced himself from that life"."I hope the verdict would bring some comfort to those who had lost friends and relatives," Dan tells BBC's Newsday.Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, More than 400 bodies were dug up in Shakahola forestOn Monday, Stephen Mwiti, 48, who said he had lost all six of his children to the cult, welcomed the verdict."I'm a happy man, that all persons have been convicted," he told the BBC outside court.His former wife was one of those convicted of murder alongside Mackenzie.Delivering her eight-hour judgment in the port city of Mombasa, Justice Diana Mochache said Mackenzie's followers believed he was "Jesus's mouthpiece".One of his co-accused told the court that Mackenzie had said anyone who resisted fasting must be forced to go to heaven "through kicks and blows".Burials in the forest where the cult was based were described as "weddings", with those who died celebrated as having "wedded with Jesus", the judge said.Mackenzie and other cult leaders also face separate cases involving terrorism, radicalisation and denying children an education.The murder verdict is the first ruling on the most serious charges against the pastor, who was arrested in 2023 after more than 400 bodies were discovered in shallow graves in Shakahola forest, near Kenya's coast.He is due to be sentenced on 6 November.Additional reporting by Thomas MukhwanaMore about the cult from the BBC:

sources.headline: Kenyan starvation cult leader guilty of murder of 190 children and one adult
sources.text: A Kenyan court has found the starvation cult leader Paul Mackenzie and about 30 others guilty of murder over the deaths of ⁠190 children and one adult in one of the world’s worst cult-related disasters in recent history.Mackenzie was arrested in 2023 after police received a tipoff, and weeks later authorities began uncovering bodies in shallow graves in the Shakahola forest near the coast ⁠in south-eastern Kenya.Prosecutors say Mackenzie and ⁠his Good News International Church organised ​a Christian doomsday sect in which they ordered followers to starve themselves and their children to death to go to heaven before the world ended.Mackenzie denied murder charges, saying he did not force the victims to starve but the ⁠court rejected that argument.In total, more than 400 bodies have been recovered from the Shakahola forest. Many were severely decomposed, and only 26 of them were able to be identified.Monday’s judgment covered 191 deaths while investigations into the other deaths are continuing.Justice Diana Kavedza Mochache said in a hearing lasting more than eight hours that in some cases children were isolated and denied food while their parents watched.Kenyan high court judge Diana Kavedza Mochache on 19 October. Photograph: EPAMackenzie was in ​court, wearing a striped polo shirt and red trousers, sitting alongside his wife, ‌one of the co-accused.He was silent, ‌staring into space before the ruling was handed down.Relatives of some of those who died in the forest gathered to hear the judgment at Mombasa high ‌court.Francis Wanje, 62, lost eight family members including two grandchildren to the cult.Speaking before the verdict, he said: “It has been really a heavy thing [for] us as a family, and it has really taken us very far in terms of psychological problems … I was hoping for this particular day.”The Shakahola tragedy has gripped Kenya since the discovery of mass graves in the coastal forest more than three years ago.It raised questions over how Mackenzie was able to continue to operate despite having been on the radar of the authorities since 2017 when his premises were searched by police. In 2019, authorities shut down Mackenzie’s church and he relocated ‌to the Shakahola forest, police said.A Kenyan national youth service officer talks to a woman while on guard at the entrance to the Mombasa law courts on Monday 19 October. Photograph: Simon Maina/AFP/Getty ImagesThe case has also led to calls for tougher oversight of churches and other religious organisations in a country where religious faith plays a prominent role in public life.Kenya’s president, William Ruto, said in 2023 that government agencies should have been ​able to prevent the deaths. He said he took responsibility as president.People with direct knowledge of the cult’s activities said Mackenzie planned the mass starvation in three phases: first children, then women and young men, and finally the remaining men.Mackenzie, a former taxi driver, forbade cult members from sending their children to school and from going to hospital when they were ill, describing such institutions as satanic, some of his followers told Reuters for a 2023 article.Cult members lived in makeshift homes of polythene ⁠sheeting and thatch that Mackenzie divided into areas with biblical names such as Jerusalem and Judea.Paul Mackenzie and his co-accused during their court appearance on 19 October. Photograph: Simon Maina/AFP/Getty ImagesThe plight of his followers began ​to emerge in mid-March 2023, when a local man told ​police that his brother and wife had starved their children ​to death in the forest on Mackenzie’s orders.Mackenzie was arrested but released on bail, after which relatives say he brought forward the date ​on which he told his followers the ‌world would end. Police ​arrested him again in April 2023 and ​started combing through the forest more systematically and began exhuming mass graves.Mackenzie faces other charges over the forest deaths including terrorism-related ones, which he has denied.Prosecutors say while he was in detention he also directed the deaths of 52 people in Kwa Binzaro village, about 18 miles (30km) from Shakahola. Mackenzie has pleaded not guilty in that case.

sources.headline: Doomsday cult leader found guilty of murdering 190 children and one adult
sources.text: Doomsday cult leader Paul Mackenzie, his wife Rhoda Maweu, and 29 other co-accused have been found guilty of the murder of 190 children and one adult.

sources.headline: Starvation cult leader found guilty of murder of 190 children
sources.text:
Updated on: October 19, 2026 / 2:54 PM EDT
/ CBS/AFP
Add CBS News on Google
A self-proclaimed Kenyan preacher and his associates were found guilty of murdering 191 people, all but one of them children, in an infamous starvation cult by a Mombasa court on Monday."I am satisfied that the prosecution has proved the case against all the 29 accused persons for the murder of 190 children and one adult," the judge said.Hundreds of bodies have been discovered since 2023 at the cult base inland from the Kenyan beach resort of Malindi, in what became known as the "Shakahola Forest Massacre." Paul Mackenzie is alleged to have incited his acolytes to starve to death in order to "meet Jesus."Mackenzie and his associates pleaded not guilty to 191 counts of murder in 2024. He has also denied charges of manslaughter and terrorism in separate cases.The Office of the Director of Public Prosecutions welcomed the "momentous" verdict, with director Renson Ingonga telling reporters: "Getting a conviction of such counts...is not something that comes that easily." In the three years since the grisly discovery, more bodies of children, women and men have been unearthed, bringing the total to well over 400.
Self-proclaimed pastor Paul Mackenzie looks on during his court appearance at the Mombasa Law Court in Mombasa on Oct. 19, 2026.
SIMON MAINA /AFP via Getty Images
Mackenzie looked impassive as he arrived at Mombasa Law Courts on Monday with 29 other accused, who descended from a barred-window bus handcuffed in pairs.
Relatives of the victims were also in court, many making their way to Mombasa from rural communities along the coast.Francis Wanje, 62, lost eight family members, including his daughter and two grandchildren, in Shakahola."This day, to me, is a very, very important day," he told AFP before the session started."We are expecting a ruling that will be a lesson to the whole public, so that such kinds of things will not happen again," he said, expressing anger over the initial government inaction.
There have been calls in Kenya for tougher regulations on religious organizations after it emerged that Mackenzie had been arrested twice in the past but released.The prosecution alleges that Mackenzie "initiated and directed" extreme fasting at his 800-acre ranch in Shakahola Forest, claiming there was a "structured hierarchy of death" which said children should die first, followed by teenagers, women and then men.The children mostly died from starvation, but also from "asphyxia, neck compression and traumatic head injury," prosecutors said, based on postmortems and police reports.Mackenzie's lawyers said the case was "largely founded on circumstantial evidence, hearsay accounts and inconclusive forensic findings."Case exposedMackenzie was arrested in April 2023, after a rights group tipped off authorities and some followers were rescued.The subsequent police operation exposed hundreds of shallow graves, with a soaring death toll that required a pause in excavations as local morgues ran out of space.The Kenya National Commission on Human Rights said in 2024 that the death toll was 429. Some victims are still unidentified.
In January, Mackenzie was charged over another 52 bodies found at a nearby village.
The exhumed bodies of victims of a religious cult are laid out in the village of Shakahola, near the coastal city of Malindi, in southern Kenya Sunday, April 23, 2023.
AP
The self-styled pastor has a history of extremism and evaded law enforcement for years.He established the Good News International Church in 2003, and set up branches in Nairobi and along Kenya's coast that attracted thousands of devotees, though he claimed it closed in 2019.Followers have told their families and officials they believed Mackenzie when he preached that starvation was the path to salvation. He allegedly split members into smaller groups assigned biblical names. It's believed these smaller groups died together and were buried together in mass graves.State pathologists have said many of the exhumed victims died of starvation, but some showed signs of strangulation.Mackenzie was arrested in 2017 over charges of "radicalization" but was acquitted. He was arrested again in 2019 in relation to two child deaths at Shakahola, but released on bail.Investigators have said Mackenzie was a taxi driver in the early 2000s, before he created the Good News International Ministry. Locals have said he quickly drew followers with fiery sermons at his church on the coast in Malindi, then from across Kenya with his online presence.
Several surviving members of the group have told family members that what he preached would often come true, citing as an example his prediction that "a great virus" would come, just before COVID-19 hit the country. As people struggled during the pandemic, financially and medically, Mackenzie preached about leaving the difficulties of life behind and "turning to salvation."

Published: 11:51pm, 19 Oct 2026Updated: 1:31pm, 20 Oct 2026

Starvation cult leader Paul Mackenzie and 28 others were found guilty of murder by a Kenyan court on Monday over the deaths of 190 children and an adult in one of the world’s worst cult-related tragedies in recent history.

The preacher was arrested in 2023 after police received a tip-off, and weeks later authorities began uncovering bodies in shallow graves in the Shakahola Forest near the coast in southeastern Kenya.

Prosecutors say ‌Mackenzie and his Good News International Church organised a Christian doomsday sect in which they ordered followers to starve themselves and their children to death to go to heaven before the world ended.

The case has gripped Kenya since the discovery of the mass graves.

It raised questions over how Mackenzie was able to continue to operate despite having been on the radar of the authorities since 2017 when his premises were searched by police. In 2019, authorities shut down Mackenzie’s church and he relocated to the Shakahola Forest, police said.

Mackenzie denied murder charges, saying he did not force the victims to starve, but the court rejected that argument.

A mass gravesite in Shakahola in 2023. Photo: AFP

He and the others convicted will be sentenced on November 6. Defence lawyer Lawrence Obonyo, who represents Mackenzie and almost all ⁠of the others convicted, said he had been instructed to appeal.

In total, more than 400 bodies have ‌been recovered from the Shakahola Forest.

Many of the children’s bodies were severely decomposed, with only 26 able to be identified, and investigations into the other deaths were ongoing.

Justice Diana ⁠Kavedza Mochache said in a hearing lasting more ⁠than eight hours that in some cases children were isolated and denied food while their parents watched.

The director of public prosecutions, Renson Ingonga, told reporters afterwards at the Mombasa High Court: “That is the best judgment we would ever get”.

Mackenzie was in court, wearing a striped polo shirt and red trousers, sitting alongside his wife, one of the co-accused.

Exhumed bodies of cult victims in the Shakahola Forest, Kenya, in 2023. Photo: AFP

When his name was read out by the judge, he was silent, staring into space.

The case has led to calls for tougher oversight ‌of churches and ‌other religious organisations in a country where religious faith plays a prominent role in public life.

Kenyan President William Ruto said in 2023 that government agencies should have been able to prevent the deaths. ‌He said he took responsibility as president.

People with direct knowledge of the cult’s activities have told Reuters that Mackenzie planned the mass starvation in three phases: first children, then women and ⁠young men, and finally the remaining men.

A former taxi driver, Mackenzie forbade cult members from sending their children to school and from going to hospital when they were ill, branding such institutions as satanic, relatives of ⁠some of his victims told Reuters for a 2023 article.

Cult members lived in makeshift homes of polythene sheeting and thatch that Mackenzie divided into areas with biblical names like Jerusalem and Judea.

The plight of his followers began to emerge in mid-March 2023, when a local man told police that his brother and wife had starved their children to death in ‌the forest on Mackenzie’s orders.

Mackenzie was arrested but released ‌on bail, after which relatives say he brought forward the date on which he told his followers the world would end. Police arrested him again in April 2023 and started combing through the forest more systematically and began exhuming mass graves.

Mackenzie faces other charges over the forest deaths including terrorism-related ones, which he has denied.

Prosecutors say while he was in detention he also directed the deaths of 52 people in Kwa Binzaro village, which lies about 30km (18 miles) from Shakahola. Mackenzie has pleaded not guilty in that case.
